●      Osteocytes = osteoblasts (mesenchymal cells) that have been internalized within lacunar spaces of mineralized bone

●      Play key role in bone homeostasis

●      Likely induce osteoclast and osteoblast activity in response to bone injury

●      Undergo apoptosis with aging

What are Osteoclasts? Where are they located? What is their origin and physiological role?

●      Osteoclast, HP stem cell derived

●      Resides with Howship lacunae along periphery of bony trabeculae

●      Multinucleated, bone-resorbing cell of monocyte/macrophage lineage (not mesenchymal, like osteoblasts)

Prominent bone remodeling is normal in what age group?

●      Children

●      Substantial amounts of unmineralized osteoid in specimens from infants and very young children

Thicker bony trabeculae and greater bone remodeling is normally seen in what gender and age?

●      Adolescent/young adult males - compared with females and older adults

What is osteopenia, when do we call is "osteoporosis"?

●      Osteopenia = thinning of bony trabeculae

●      Represents an imbalance of bone homeostasis, with reduced new bone formation

●      Termed osteoporosis → if generalized and associated with reduced bone density testing

●      Osteopenia

What is osteolysis

●      Discrete area of excessive osteoclast-induced bone resorption

●      Thinning of bone here = osteolysis

What is osteonecrosis

●      Nonviable bony trabeculae with loss of osteocytes within lacunar spaces

●      May be associated with necrosis of medullary (HP) cavity

●      Associated with bone marrow infiltration by neoplasms

○      Most common in acute lymphoblastic leukemia


●      Central core of necrotic bone (closed arrows), surrounded by new bone: open arrow

What is osteosclerosis? What is it often associated with?

●      Thickened bony trabeculae that may be anastomosing

●      Radiographically apparent when generalized and prominent

●      Often associated with fibrosis

Osteosclerosis is linked to neoplastic and nonneoplastic disorders of bone and bone marrow
Give 3 neoplastic examples

●      Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) including primary myelofibrosis

●      POEMS

●      Systemic mastocytosis

●      Osteoblastic metastases (prostate and breast carcinoma)

What bone changes may be seen in renal osteodystrophy

●      Variable features of bony trabeculae and BM stroma during course of chronic renal disease

●      Spectrum of sequelae from low and high bone turnover

●      Bone erosion, bone formation , and quiescent phases

●      May see bony trabecular changes linked to secondary hyperparathyroidism

●      May see changes linked to osteomalacia with defective mineralization

●      May see bone islands within medullary space

●      Increased osteoclastic activity in renal osteodystrophy

●      Simultaneous thinning and thickening of bone in renal osteodystrophy

What is the pathogenesis of myeloma-associated bony abnormalities

●      Complex pathogenesis via interactions of myeloma cells with BM cells

●      Myeloma cells affect mesenchymal stem cells and other BM stromal cells

○      Suppressed osteoblastogenesis → due to inhibitors secreted by myeloma cells

○      Increased osteoclastogenesis → due to osteoblast deactivation and production of osteoclast-activating factors

○      Osteoclasts produce factors that stimulate myeloma cells

What is osteomalacia 

●      Excessive osteoid formation with defective mineralization

●      Linked to selected renal disorders

●      Constitutional and acquired types



What changes are seen with Paget disease of the bone

●      Increased osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity

○      Disorganized woven bone

●      May be familial

Photo: see the disordered whorls

 

What is osteopetrosis - What are the typical changes  

●      Constitutional disorder caused by mutations in genes expressing proteins linked to osteoclastic bone resorption

●      Markedly expanded and confluent bony trabeculae with increased bone density and dramatically reduced HP space

Bone Homeostasis is controlled by complex mechanisms - What are the cellular and non-cellular factors necessary for healthy bone homeostasis?

●      Cellular:

○      Normal numbers & function of osteoblasts, osteoclasts, osteocytes, vasculature, stem cells

●      Non-cellular:

○      Adequate calcium phosphorus, vitamin D, and and regulatory factors required (stem cell factor, growth factors, IL-3,4,5,6)

What age-related factor is linked to osteocyte apoptosis and loss of regulation of bone remodeling by osteocytes

●      Estrogen deficiency in women is linked to osteocyte apoptosis and loss of regulation of bone remodeling by osteocytes

Osteopenia/osteoporosis is very common in what gender and age group 

●      Elderly, especially postmenopausal women

Rare constitutional disorders, such as osteopetrosis and some types of osteomalacia, generally manifest in what age group

●      During infancy and early childhood - Severe HP compromise is characteristic

What features should you be looking for when you assess the trabecular bone in a BM trephine biopsy   

●      1) Assessment of adequacy

○      Must be at least 1 cm in length

○      Must show intact, not crushed, bony trabeculae and medullary cavity

●      2) Assessment of bony trabeculae

○      Assess thickness, uniformity, and contours of bony trabeculae

○      Assess for relative proportions of osteoid and mineralized bone including osteoid seams and cement lines

○      Assess for thickening and anastomoses of bony trabeculae

○      Assess lacunar spaces for intact, viable osteocytes or empty lacunar spaces in nonviable bony trabeculae

○      Assess for tiny disconnected strands of bony trabeculae (bone islands)

○      Assess for composite/mixed features of thickened and thinned bony trabeculae with bone islands

■      Typical feature of chronic renal disease

■      Bone islands are disconnected thin segments of bony trabeculae within medullary space

○      Assess for evidence of osteosis fibrosa cystica

■      Islands of osteoblasts and stroma within bony trabeculae

○      Assess for osteoblast rimming

■      Number and extent

○      Assess for osteoclasts

■      Number

■      Howship lacunae localization

●      3) Access for associated fibrosis &/or necrosis of medullary cavity

○      Assess for other BM stromal abnormalities

○      Osteopenia common in severely ill patients with gelatinous transformation (serous fat atrophy)

●      4) Assess for common neoplasms linked to pathology of bony trabeculae

○      Carcinoma

○      Myeloma

○      MPN, primary myelofibrosis, and mastocytosis

When you are assessing bony trabeculae, what patient factors do you need to consider

●      Correlate appearance of bony trabeculae with normal features based on age and sex

What underlying disease/cause should you consider if BOTH thickened AND markedly thinned bony trabeculae are present, especially if associated with bone islands

●      Chronic renal disease

What underlying disease/cause should you consider if bony trabeculae are thickened with disorganized swirls of haphazard bone

●      Paget disease

167 Metastatic Carcinoma and Sarcoma involving the BM

 

Name 5 common non-hematologic tumors involving bone marrow in adults    

●      Carcinomas of prostate, breast, lung, and gastrointestinal origins

●      Melanoma

●      Neuroblastoma, and Rhabdomyosarcoma

Name 4 common non hematologic tumors involving bone marrow in children. Which is most common?    

●      Neuroblastoma (most common)

●      Ewing sarcoma/peripheral neuroectodermal tumor

●      Retinoblastoma

●      Rhabdomyosarcoma

What is the term for circulating non hematological tumor cells in blood    

●      Carcinocythemia

Name 4 possible PB Morphologic Findings you might see with Metastatic Carcinoma or Sarcoma involving the BM    

●      Leukoerythroblastic reaction

○      Increased "teardrop" red blood cells

●      Leukemoid reaction

○      Leukocytosis due to cytokines produced by tumor

○      WCC > 50 x 10^9/L

●      Cytopenias

○      Anemia and thrombocytopenia

●      Microangiopathic hemolytic picture

○      Secondary to mucin in metastatic adenocarcinoma

○      Can also be seen secondary to therapeutic agents (mitomycin C)

●      Circulating tumor cells (carcinoma or sarcoma)

○      Rarely detected in breast & small cell carcinoma of lung

○      Carcinocythemia

Name 4 possible Morphologic Findings you might see in the BM with Metastatic Carcinoma and Sarcoma infiltration    

●      1) BM aspirate may contain metastatic carcinoma/sarcoma cells

○      Low yield due to tumor-associated fibrosis

●      2) BM touch imprints

○      Higher yield in detecting metastatic tumor cells compared to aspirate smears

●      3) BM trephine biopsy

○      Provides highest yield for detection of metastatic disease

○      Patchy/focal distribution of some metastases

○      Need adequate length

○      Metastatic carcinoma usually inaspirable (dry tap)

○      Desmoplastic stromal response

○      Severe marrow fibrosis (may mask sparse carcinoma cells if fibrosis is extensive)

○      Bone changes: sclerotic bone and bone resorption

○      Single cells or small cohesive clusters with nuclear molding or rosetting

Which IHC stain supports epithelial origin    

●      Cytokeratin (CK) expression in metastatic bone marrow deposits supports epithelial origin

Which IHC stain supports breast or female genital tract origin    

●      Estrogen receptor (ER) hormone expression

Which 2 IHC stains supports neuroendocrine origin    

●      Chromogranin and synaptophysin expression

Which IHC stain supports pulmonary origin in patient with known lung cancer    

●      Expression of thyroid transcription factor (TTF-1)

Ewing's Sarcoma (PNET) typically expresses what IHC markers    

●      CD99 and FLI-1 and variably NSE and neurofilaments

●      Note: coexpression of CD99 not specific for ES/PNET and can be seen in other tumors e.g. T cell lymphoma

What are 4 IHC stains for rhabdomyosarcoma?

 

●      Muscle specific actin

●      Desmin

●      Myogenin

●      MyoD1

 



What 2 stains could prove useful in separating neuroblastoma from other mimics 

●      S100 protein and NSE

Cytological description of neuroblasts 

●      Uniform, small, blue cells with hyperchromatic to vesicular chromatin and scant, eosinophilic, fibrillary cytoplasm, “neuropil”

●      Look for nuclear molding

●      May form Homer-Wright rosettes



Name 2 malignancies positive for CD99    

●      Ewing sarcoma and T cell lymphoma

●      Non specific but does distinguish Ewing from neuroblastoma

Name 4 positive stains for neuroblastoma?    

●      Neuron specific enolase (NSE), CD57, CD56, Protein gene product 9.5 (PGP 9.5), synaptophysin, chromogranin, neurofilament protein, ALK-1

 

 

Non-Neoplastic WBC and Platelet Disorders

Congenital Neutropenia

Chediak-Hagashi syndrome

 

Q. Inheritance pattern of Chediak-Hagashi syndrome

Autosomal recessive

 

Q. What gene is affected in Chediak-Hagashi syndrome?

·       LYST gene on chromosome 1q42 that encodes a protein involved in intracellular trafficking of proteins

 

Q. Etiology of Chediak-Hagashi syndrome

Abnormalities of lysosome-related organelle morphology and function resulted in a microtubule polymerization defect which leads to a decrease in phagocytosis.

 

Q. Clinical presentations[QZ7] 

·       Partial oculocutaneous albinism

·       Peripheral neuropathy

·       Decrease in phagocytosis → results in recurrent pyogenic infections

·       Pancytopenia

·       HSM, lymphadenopathy

·       Lymphoid transformation of EBV infection

·       HLH in accelerated disease

 

Q. Morphological abnormalities in Chediak-Hagashi syndrome?

·       Abnormal cytoplasmic inclusions involving the white blood cells (neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils and lymphocytes)

·       Variably sized large aggregates of purple/blue/red granules

 

Q. Prognosis of Chediak-Hagashi syndrome?

·       Most patients die by ten years of age

Transplant topics

Cellular basis of hematopoiesis and stem cell transplantation

 

Q. What are the key properties of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs)?

 

1. Extensive self-renewal capability → asymmetrical cell division

2. Differentiation into all blood cell types (pluripotent)

 

What is asymmetrical cell division?

 

●      An asymmetric cell division produces two daughter cells with different cellular fates.

●      This is in contrast to symmetric cell divisions which give rise to daughter cells of equivalent fates.

●      Notably, stem cells divide asymmetrically to give rise to two distinct daughter cells: one copy of the original stem cell as well as a second daughter programmed to differentiate into a non-stem cell fate.

●      Note: in times of growth or regeneration, stem cells can also divide symmetrically, to produce two identical copies of the original cell

 




Q. How many primitive HSCs are present in the BM and what are their features?

 

●      The most primitive HSCs are rare, approximately 1 in 10^4-10^6 BM cells (1 in a million)

○      Adult HSCs cycle slowly

○      Present in G0 phase

○      Resistant to cytokine stimulation

○      Their daughter cells may either be a replicate of the parent cells (self-renewal) or enter into a differentiation program → asymmetrical cell division

 

What general changes take place as hematopoietic stem cells undergo differentiation?

 

●      Differentiation through progenitor hierarchy

●      Pluri-ptent - Multi-potent - oligo-potent - mono-potent progenitors

●      Loss of self-renewal capacity

●      Increased restriction in differentiation potential

 

What regulates hematopoietic cell development?

 

●      Signals provided by the BM microenvironment

●      Heterologous cells (mesenchymal, endothelial, neural)

●      Hematopoietic cells

●      Extracellular matrix cells

 



 

What are 3 sources of stem cells for clinical purposes?

 

●      1. Umbilical cord blood

●      2. Mobilized peripheral blood stem cells (apheresis collection following a mobilization phase) - GCSF, Plerixafor, Cyclophosphamide

●      3. Bone marrow stem cells from harvest

Are there any survival differences between using PB and BM as a source of HSPCs in adults? Children?

 

●      Adults - NO

●      Children - ? YES - more studies needed

●      Retrospective study showed poorer outcomes for children with PB grafts

 

What are the differences for the recipient between PB and BM harvest for transplantation in adults vs children?

 

●      PB

○      Minimal short-medium term toxicities

○      More rapid engraftment

○      Lower risk of graft failure (more CD34+ cells)

○      Fewer earlier complications

○      More frequent chronic GVHD (T-cells)

○      Children had poorer outcomes

●      BM

○      More graft failure

○      Lower rates of acute and chronic GVHD

■      May be superior for non-malignant cases due to lower GVHD

○      More RBCs and plasma (requires modification in ABO mismatch transplant)

■      Plasma or RBC reduce!

 

What are the HLAs in MHC I and MHCII?

 

●      MHC I

○      HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C

○      “I” = think HLA plus 1 letter

●      MHC II

○      HLA DR, HLA DQ, HLA DP, HLA DM, HLA DO

○      “II” = think HLA plus 2 letters

 

Note: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC), group of genes that code for proteins found on the surfaces of cells that help the immune system recognize foreign substances. MHC proteins are found in all higher vertebrates. In human beings the complex is also called the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) system

 

What cells have MHC I? MHC II?

 

●      MHC I - all cells

●      MHC II - Antigen presenting cells

 

What type of donor/HLA matching is the #1 choice?

 

●      Complete HLA-matched sibling donor

 

Why is a sibling donor the #1 choice?

 

●      HLA-matched sibling donors create less GVHD

●      Due to higher chance of match at → minor histocompatibility sites

●      Less morbidity and mortality

 

Note: Minor histocompatibility antigen (also known as MiHA) are receptors on the cellular surface of donated organs that are known to give an immunological response in some organ transplants. They cause problems of rejection less frequently than those of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC).

 

Which HLAs do we match at (5)?

 

●      HLA I - A, B, C

●      HLA II - DRB1, DQB1

 

Note: 2 alleles for each

 

What is a 10/10 HLA match?

 

●      Match for both alleles at HLA- A, B, C

●      HLA DRB1, DQB1

 

If a 10/10 match is not possible, what is acceptable?

 

●      Single mismatch is acceptable

 

Why do unrelated donors have a higher risk of GVHD than related, even if 10/10 match?

 

●      Unrelated donors more likely to be mismatch at minor histocompatibility antigens

●      Therefore increased risk of GVHD, and increased immunosuppression needed

 

What are other types of stem cells that can be used if there is no HLA-matched donor?

 

●      1. Haploidentical donors

●      2. Umbilical cord blood

 

Note: A haploidentical, or half-matched, donor is usually your mom, your dad or your child. Parents are always a half-match for their children. Siblings (brothers or sisters) have a 50% (1 out of 2) chance of being a half-match for each other.

 

What are the advantages of using cord blood for stem cells?

 

●      1. Less stringent matching

○      Fewer T-cells and T-cells are naive

○      Only need 4/6 match for cord blood

●      2. Quicker

○      Useful if urgent SCT needed

 

What are the disadvantages of using cord blood for stem cells?

 

●      1. Slow rate of engraftment

●      2. Prolonged myelosuppression

●      3. Delayed immune reconstitution

●      4. Higher rates of death from infection

 

What can be done to mitigate the risk of cord blood stem cells?

 

●      1. Use 2 cords with an adequate cell dose

●      2. Methods to expand numbers within UCB donation



Which chemokines determine the rate, timing, and destination of the HSC that circulate from the BM to periphery?

 

●      CXCL12 and its receptor CXCR4

●      Integrins, particularly Very Late Antigen-4 (VLA-4, also termed integrin a4b1)

●      Selectins, such as P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1 (PSGL1, also termed CD162) and the calcium-sensing receptor

●      Intracellular-signaling molecules, Gas and Rac1/Rac2

 

Name three agents to mobilize HSCs for apheresis collection?

 

1-     GCSF

2-     Chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide)

3-     Plerixafor

 

What is the mechanism of G-CSF mobilization?

 

●      Reduction of the SDF-1 (CXCL12) transcripts + proteolytic cleavage of the protein

●      Evasion of phagocytosis by increased CD47 expression

 

Mechanism of action of plerixafor? Is it used alone or in combination with G-CSF?

 

●      Plerixafor blocks the chemokine receptor CXCR4 from binding to CXCL12

●      It’s used in combination with G-CSF

 

Note: plerixafor acts as an antagonist (or perhaps more accurately a partial agonist) of the alpha chemokine receptor CXCR4 and an allosteric agonist of CXCR7. The CXCR4 alpha-chemokine receptor and one of its ligands, SDF-1, are important in hematopoietic stem cell homing to the bone marrow and in hematopoietic stem cell quiescence

 

What is the surrogate marker for HSCs?

 

●      Enumeration of CD34 cells

 

What are the minimum number of CD34+ cells/kg required for transplantation? In PB, BM, UCB??

 

●      1) PB/BM

○      >2 x 10^6 CD34+ cells /kg (> 2 million/kg)

○      Improved survival in unrelated transplants

○      > 8 x 10^6 PB are associated with increased GVHD (too much of a good thing)

●      2) UCB

○      Minimal dose is >2.5 x 10^7 nucleated cells/kg or >1.7 x 10^5 CD34+ cells/kg (170,000) - (? round to 200, 000 = might be easier number to remember with 2 million for PB/BM)

What is the relationship between the degree of mismatch, and the number of HSCs needed?

 

●      Greater the degree of mismatch, higher the dose needed

 

What are the advantages/ disadvantages of a sibling donor?

 

Advantages of a sibling donor:

·       Better match at HLA and minor histocompatibility loci

o   Reduced chance of GVHD compared to unrelated donor cell sources.

·       Donor cells can potentially be obtained quickly.

·       Potentially, donor can be easily approached again for additional HSPCs to improve graft function or for T-cells for donor lymphocyte infusion to augment alloimmune response against recipient disease cells.

Disadvantages of a sibling donor

·       Potentially less graft-versus-disease immune response

·       I.e. the opposite of the advantage mentioned above (Reduced chance of GVHD compared to unrelated donor cell sources)

 

What are the advantages and disadvantages of an unrelated donor?

 

Advantages of an unrelated donor

·       Increased graft versus disease compared to sibling donor.
Donors available for common haplotypes.

Disadvantages of an unrelated donor

·       Increased graft versus host response compared to sibling donor.

·       Potentially more difficult to obtain additional HSPCs and donor lymphocytes for graft failure, and increased allo-immune response against recipient disease cells.

 

What are the advantages/disadvantages of a Haploidentical donor?

Advantages of a haploidentical donor
• Donor cells commonly available.
• Increased graft versus disease.
• Potentially, donor can be easily approached again for additional HSPCs to improve graft function or for T-cells for donor lymphocyte infusion to augment alloimmune response against recipient disease cells.

Disadvantages of a haploidentical donor
• More immunosuppression required given the greater HLA mismatch.

What are the advantages/disadvantages of a cord blood graft?

Advantages of cord blood
• Donor cells available when other cell sources not available.
• Donor cells quickly available.

Disadvantages of cord blood
• Longer time to engraftment.
• Longer time for immune reconstitution.

What are sites of hematopoiesis at the different stages of gestational age?

 

●      1- Yolk sac →  3-6 wks of gestation

●      2- Fetal Liver →  6-20 wks of gestation

●      3- Bone marrow →  20 wks and onward

●      Note: dorsal route aorta → after yolk sac

 

What make HSCs resistant to multiple chemotherapeutic agents (2)?

                            

●      1- Since HSCs are relatively quiescent and do not divide actively they get spared by antimetabolite drugs e.g flurouracil

●      2- HSCs express high levels of the verapamil-sensitive multidrug-resistance membrane efflux pump (P-glycoprotein), which confers resistance to multiple chemotherapeutic agents

 

Which dye can be used to identify the HSCs in flow cytometry?

 

●      Rhodamine-123 or Hoechst-33342 dyes = The HSC efflux pump excludes certain fluorescent dyes

●      Using these dyes in combination with flow cytometry, it has been possible to identify a population of hematopoietic cells with low dye retention, so-called side population (SP) cells.

●      Although this population is markedly enriched for HSCs, SP cells still represent a heterogeneous mix and are not equivalent to pure HSCs.

What is the immunophenotype of HSCs?

 

●      CD34+, CD38−, Lin−, CD45RA−, Thy1+, Rho(lo), CD49f+

●      Lin = lineage specific markers

 

What percentage of BM cells express CD34?

 

●      Early studies to isolate humans HSCs found that approximately 1% of human BM cells express CD34.

 

 

ISHAGE Protocol for CD34 Enumeration

 

What is the name of the guidelines used for stem cell enumeration?

●      International Society of Hematotherapy and Graft Engineering

○      Established stem cell enumeration committee to validate a flow cytometric method to quantitate CD34+ cells in PB and aphaeresis products

What are the two methods for Stem cell enumeration? And how are they done?

●      Four parameter two colour panel had been proposed

○      1) Dual platform initially (still at VGH)

■      Uses two analyzers to calculate number of CD34+ cells in a sample

■      1) CBC analyzer to enumerate WBC

■      2) Flow cytometry analyzer to provide the % of CD34+ events (stem cells)

■      The absolute number of CD34+ events is calculated using the denominator of the WBC from the CBC analyzer

○      2) Single Platform (BCCH)

■      Only the flow cytometer is used to provide the CD34+ count

■      Number of kits available using → fluorospheres/beads

■      A known volume and concentration of beads added to the equal volume of the patients sample

■      By mixing known amount of beads with a blood sample, the absolute count is derived directly from the flow cytometer by measuring the → ratio beads and the CD34+ cells in the sample

What are the criteria for identification of true CD34+ cells?

●      Moderate CD45 antigen characteristic of blast cells (lower level than lymphocytes and monocytes)

●      Moderate to strong intensity of CD34 antigen

●      Low side scatter (SS) pattern and Low to intermediate forward angle light scatter(FS) characteristics of blast cells

○      CD34++, CD45+, mod FS and low SS

 

ISHAGE Guidelines Specimen Requirements

●      Specimen requirements

○      ACD and EDTA anti coagulated samples

○      Storage and transport at RT to avoid hemolysis

○      Analyze ASAP, within 24 hours

■      PMNs begin to die. If wait too long, then there will be an artifactual increase in CD34+ cells (denominator will be smaller)

What is the Analysis Protocol for ISHAGE?

●      Analysis Protocol

○      Three tubes: CD45-FITC/CD34-PE x2 (in duplicate), and CD45-FITC/Isotype-PE

■      Wash-out in between (Normal Saline) to ensure no carryover

○      Collect 75,000 CD45+ events and 100 CD34+

●      Sequential gating technique

○      Plot 1: CD45 vs SS

■      To gate out CD45 negative, and to gate on the lymphocytes

○      Plot 2: CD34 vs SSC staining of CD45+

■      To get only events that are 34+

○      Plot 3: CD45 vs SSC of the CD34+ cells

■      To clean up the CD34+ cells that are truly the blast cells based on the dim45

○      Plot 4: Light scatter (FSC/SSC) of CD34+ events

●      Calculate the CD34+ = P2 and P3 and P4 (as below!)

 

 

●      Note: Plot 5 with P6 is an estimate of the % of CD34+ cells if you did not do the ISHAGE protocol!

●      Also, we do a viability dye (ie. 7-AAD) and only include the viable cells

 

 

How do you calculate the CD34+ cells in the Dual platform method?

 

●      CD34 % x WBC = absolute CD34/volume (cells/uL)

 

Transfusion in Transplant

What are the types of Mismatch?

●      Major Mismatch

○      Recipient has antibody that will react with the donors antigen

■      Example: A donor into O recipient

■      O recipient plasma has Anti-A and Anti- B

○      ie. Major is immediate! (Recipient can lyse)

●      Minor

○      Donor has an antibody that will react with recipient antigen

■      Example is O donor into A/B

●      Bidirectional

○      Both Major and Minor

○      Combination of A and B in donor and recipient

■      Eg A into B or the opposite

Can we have mismatches in Solid Organ Transplantation? How?

●      Yes

○      Endothelium has A, B or AB

●      Therefore, ABO compatibility is important in Solid organ transplant

○      Major mismatch can cause → rapid rejection → endothelial damage

○      We don’t usually do this… but if there is no other choice, can do isohemagglutinin titre?

●      O is universal donor!!

●      MAJOR INCOMPATIBLE LIVING DONOR RENAL ALLOGRAFT

○      Major ABO mismatch failures...

○      Based on isohemagglutinin titre

○      Protocol driven management peri-transplant

■      Pre-transplant PLEX

■      Post-transplant PLEX

■      Intense immunosuppression

Is HLA or ABO important in Stem cell transplant vs. Solid organ/ Why?

●      HLA important in both

●      ABO is important only in solid organ

○      Because the stem cell do not have A, B, or H antigens!

■      It may impact the transplant, but not get in the same way

What is Passenger Lymphocyte Hemolysis?

●      May occur with minor incompatible solid organ transplant

●      Review of minor

○      Donor has an antibody that will react with recipient antigen

■      Example is O donor into A/B

●      Passenger Lymphocyte Hemolysis

○      Viable donor lymphocytes in graft can produce Ab

○      These can coat recipient endogenous RBCs causing → extravascular hemolysis

●      Our role in TM is to not make it worse

For Solid Organ transplant, what blood do you transfuse post-transplant and Why?

●      Selection of RBC pos-transplant is to avoid exacerbation of passenger lymphocyte hemolysis

●      Therefore match to the → donor

Stem cell transplant

 

What are basics to consider for TM in SC transplant?

●      Patient tracking in LIS

●      ABO type of donors and recipient

●      Ab screen status - alloimmunized patient

●      Receipt and handling of local/external stem cell product

●      Impact on use of TML automation

○      Ineligible for computer XM

●      Inventory supply

○      Especially platelets

●      Platelet refractoriness

○      +/- HLA matched platelets

●      Engraftment and group switching

●      Communication with home hospital

 

What are the 3 phases of Transplant, and what are the blood product considerations?

●      1) Pre-transplant

○      Leukocyte reduction (done at CBS)

■      Reduces HLA-alloimmunization (TRAP study)

■      CMV Safe

■      Estimated risk of <1:13.6 million with LR product

○      Avoidance of directed donations

○      Gamma irradiation

■      Stem cell transplants

●      2) Peri-transplant

○      Information on dates, conditioning, groups of donor and recipient

○      Confirmation of support capability

○      Confirmation of updated patient TMS file

○      Last group and screen of recipient <7 days prior to SCT

○      Infusion confirmation

●      3) Post-transplant

○      Pre engraftment and engraftment affects ABO matching of products

What do you need to do to BM vs. PB vs. Cord stem cell sources for a Major vs. Minor mismatch?

●      BM stem cell source

○      Major ABO mismatch - Red cell deplete

■      Don’t want to transfuse out of group RBCs

○      Minor ABO mismatch - plasma deplete

■      Don’t want to transfuse the antibodies

○      Bidirectional - both RBC and plasma deplete

●      PB stem cell sources (Aphaeresis)

○      Hematocrit kept <2%, typically ~10mL

○      Considered Red cell and plasma depleted at source

●      Cord stem cell source

○      Usually red cell and plasma depleted prior to cryo-storage

■      Otherwise have to wash with dextran/albumin to remove lysed RBCs and donor plasma post-thaw

Red cell depletion

●      Red cell depletion: RBC depletion has minimal CD34+ loss

●      In Vancouver, we red cell deplete for every Major incompatible SCT

●      Other centres:

○      Use antibody titre of the recipient to guide this

○      Some PLEX to get the titre

What are the complications of a Major ABO incompatible Stem cell transplant

  1. Acute hemolysis
    1. Can occur in major or minor incompatibility
  2. Delayed red cell engraftment
    1. Antibodies of recipient can continue up to 3-4 months
    2. ONLY impacts RBCs
    3. >40 days after Major ABO incompatible (vs. 20 days with ABO identical)
    4. Chimerism may persist for months
      1. Potential for delayed hemolysis
  3. Pure Red cell aplasia
    1. More likely if:
      1. Non-myeloablative 8-38% vs. Myeloablative transplant 16-29%
      2. A-antigen incompatibility
      3. CSA-only prophylaxis (only T cell suppression)
    2. Anti-donor isohemagglutinin tire will fall over time
    3. Case reports: EPO/plasma exchange,
  4. Peri-transplant
    1. Need product compatible with both donor and recipient

What are the complications of Minor ABO incompatible stem cell transplant

●      Acute hemolysis with stem cell infusion

○      Depends on donor titre / volume of plasma

●      Passenger lymphocyte syndrome

○      Graft’s viable lymphocytes produce isohemagglutinins / antibodies against the residual host/recipient RBC

○      DAT+, intravascular hemolysis, abrupt onset, possibly severe, usually subsides <2 weeks

○      Protect with appropriate products

How do you select pRBC and Plasma/Platelets for a Patient before engraftment in Major and Minor Mismatches?

 

 

How do you define POST engraftment:

●      TMS definition of engraftment:

○      1) NO RBC transfusion in the past 90 days

○      2) DAT negative

○      3) Forward group shows no evidence of recipient native cells!

 

 

Infections (viruses, bacteria & parasites) (2)

Infections relevant to hematology

Viruses

Note: COVID 19 will be covered in coagulation lectures

HIV

What sort of virus is HIV? DNA or RNA? -What viral family? What other virus (that is associated with hematological malignancies), belongs to this family?

●      RNA retrovirus infection

●      Retroviruses contain 2 single strands of RNA

●      Lentivirus family

●      HIV-1: 3rd identified retrovirus (after HTLV-1 and HTLV-2)

●      HIV-2: 4th identified retrovirus

At the time of initial infection, what cell type in mucous membranes or skin, does HIV infect?

●      Virus first infects Langerhans (dendritic) cells in mucous membranes or skin

What steps follow the initial HIV infection of Langerhans (dendritic) cells in mucous membranes or skin

●      Infected cells migrate to lymphoid tissues and infect CD4(+) T cells

●      Virus proliferates in T cells and destroys cells

●      HIV Nef protein regulates modulate surface proteins in infected cells = allows efficient viral replication

●      Burst of viremia within days leads to widespread tissue dissemination; targets lymphoid tissue and central nervous system

●      Symptoms of acute retroviral syndrome

Following initial infection, how is an infected host able to control viral replication  

●      Development of* immune response* by infected individual

○      Specific *CD8(+) T-cell (cytotoxic) responses* control viral replication

○      Decrease in viremia and viral load

●      Impaired cytotoxic T-cell responses occur late in infection

What information is provided by measuring CD4 counts by flow cytometric analysis

●      Marker of immunodeficiency

○      Predicts likelihood of developing AIDS and associated complications

●      Acute retroviral syndrome

○      Decreased CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells, initially

○      Increased CD8(+) T cells after several weeks, decreases CD4:CD8 ratio

●      Advanced stage (AIDS)

○      CD4(+) T-cell count < 200 cells/mm³ or < 14% of total lymphocytes

What would be the characteristic findings by flow cytometric analysis measuring CD4 counts for acute retroviral syndrome

●      Decreased CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells, initially

●      Increased CD8(+) T cells after several weeks, decreases CD4:CD8 ratio

What would be the characteristic findings by flow cytometric analysis measuring CD4 counts for Advanced stage HIV infection

●       CD4(+) T-cell count < 200 cells/mm³ or

●      < 14% of total lymphocytes

Excluding molecular testing and flow cytometry, name 1 other laboratory test relevant to hematology (hint TM) that may be abnormal with HIV infection

  1. Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test positivity
    1. Not usually associated with hemolysis
  2. Decreased serum vitamin B12 levels
    1. Not indicative of deficiency
  3. Bone marrow evaluation most informative
    1. If symptomatic patient or CD4 count < 50 cells/mm³

Peripheral Blood findings/manifestations during chronic phase of disease

●      Anemia and lymphopenia most common

●      Neutropenia

○      Effect of antiretroviral or antibiotic therapy

○      Myeloid production failure secondary to infection

●      Additional cytopenias often develop at time of AIDS-defining disease

●      Late stage: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

BM findings in HIV/AIDS - How do the findings differ between early & late disease course? 

●      Frequently hypercellular until late in disease course

○      Usually appears reactive

●      Later in disease course

○      Normocellular or hypocellular

○      Reconstitution of cell lineages after HAART therapy

○      Decreased erythroid lineage

■      Consider parvovirus if giant proerythroblasts present

○      Decreased megakaryocytes

■      Directly infected by HIV

Concurrent disorders that may be seen in the BM during AIDS infection (Hint: 3 hematological, one non-hematological neoplastic disease)

  1. Multicentric Castleman disease
    1. Plasmablasts/immunoblasts immunoreactive for HHV8-latent nuclear antigen
  2. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, plasmablastic lymphoma
    1. EBV often involved in pathogenesis
    2. Underlying immune dysregulation, cytokines, and other viruses also involved
  3. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma
    1. Bone marrow one of most common extranodal sites of disease
  4. Kaposi sarcoma rare in bone marrow

EBV and CMV: Infectious Mononucleosis Syndromes

Epstein-Barr Virus, Cytomegalovirus

 

EBV & CMV belong to what viral family    

 

●      Herpesvirus

●      Double-stranded enveloped DNA viruses

What cell type does EBV infect

 

●      Infects B cells

How does EBV infect B cells

 

●      EBV infects B cells using receptors = CD21, MHC class II

●      Majority of infected B cells are rapidly cleared from circulation in immunocompetent individuals

●      Elicits T-cell and early natural killer (NK)-cell response

Latent EBV infection occurs in what 2 cell types?

 

●      Latency established in *lymphoid cells or fibroblasts*

●      EBV genome circularizes in nucleus of B lymphocytes and is replicated as episome

●      Memory B cells remain quiescently infected and serves as reservoir for lifelong infection

What cell type does CMV infect - How does this compare with EBV?

 

●      Infects epithelial cells, endothelial cells, neuronal cells, smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, monocytes, macrophages, and T cells

●      Does not infect B cells

 

What % of clinically apparent IM are EBV vs CMV

 

●      80% cases caused by EBV

●      20% caused by CMV

 

Most common viral opportunistic infection in AIDS?    

 

●      CMV

Is primary or secondary CMV infection more common in stem cell and solid organ transplant patients      

 

●      Secondary/reactivation of virus common in stem cell or solid organ transplant patients

●      Infection occurs 1-3 months after transplant if no prophylaxis, 4-8 months if failed prophylaxis treatment

●      CMV viremia seen in 30% of at-risk pediatric lung transplant patients

Symptoms of EBV IM

 

●      Triad of sore throat, fever, lymphadenopathy

●      Symmetrical, slightly tender lymphadenopathy, especially posterior cervical region in adolescents

●      Hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, rash

●      Malaise, headache, myalgias, chills, nausea

●      Studies suggest incubation period of 30-50 days

Symptoms of CMV IM

 

●      Systemic symptoms (typhoidal)

●      Persistent fever may predominate (average duration ~ 19 days)

●      Pharyngitis and tonsillitis are rare

●      Often mild asymptomatic hepatitis

●      Lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly is uncommon

Is the heterophile antibody (monospot) test positive in both EBV & CMV IM?

 

●      No

●      Positive

○      Majority of EBV-associated IM

○      Sensitivity: 90% in adolescents, 80% in children > 4 years of age

○      EBV-specific serology unnecessary to make diagnosis of IM

○      Occasional patients with lymphoma or hepatitis have false-positive results

●      Negative

○      50% of young children with symptomatic EBV infection

○      CMV-associated IM

 

What are the 3 types of Downey atypical lymphocytes    
Most common Downey type of atypical lymphocyte associated with EBV infection?

 

●      Most common type is Downey type II cells

●      Next most common type is Downey type III cells

●      Frequently, cells intermediate between Downey type II and III cells are seen

●      Downey type I cells are most common in young children with EBV and other reactive causes

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia associated with EBV infection due to abs with what antigen specificity?

 

●      Primarily anti-i

Epstein-Barr Virus-Associated Peripheral Blood Findings

 

●      Mild to moderate leukocytosis (10-20 x 10⁹/L)

●      Lymphocytosis

○      1 week after initiation of symptoms

○      Persists up to 8 weeks

●      Atypical lymphocytes with marked heterogeneity

○      Most common type is Downey type II cells

●      Mild thrombocytopenia (< 150 x 10⁹/L) common

●      Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

○      Autoantibodies present (primarily anti-i)

○      Spherocytes and polychromasia

●      Red blood cell clumping

○      Cold agglutinin

What is the only viral infection with specific diagnostic findings in the PB

 

●      Cytomegalovirus

Cytomegalovirus-Associated Peripheral Blood Findings

 

●      Circulating infected endothelial cells typically at feather edge

●      Exclusively seen in immunocompromised patients

●      Characteristic viral inclusions not evident on Wright or Giemsa stained smears

●      Relative lymphocytosis

○      > 10% reactive lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells

○      Increased large granular lymphocytes (T and NK cells)

○      May be indistinguishable from EBV infection, but classic Downey type II cells are infrequent

●      Thrombocytopenia &/or hemolytic anemia

○      Mainly seen in children with congenital CMV infection

 

 



What Epstein-Barr Virus and Cytomegalovirus Bone Marrow Findings may be mistaken for lymphoma?       

 

●      Scattered immunoblasts

○      More common in immunodeficient individuals

○      Cells may resemble Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells

○      May also see Subtle non-necrotizing granulomas, infrequent histiocytosis

○      Rarely fibrin ring granulomas

●     

 

Parvovirus B19 (B19V) infection

 

2 synonyms for Parvovirus B19 (B19V) infection

 

●      Erythema infectiosum

●      Fifth disease

Parvovirus B19 (B19V) propagates efficiently only in what type of cell

 

●      Human erythroid progenitor cells

●      Virus is cytotoxic to cells

●      At least 4 different parvoviruses infect humans

●      Parvoviridae family; genus Erythrovirus

●      B19V is best characterized member of this family

How does B19V gain entry to cells during infection?

 

●      Virus binds blood group P antigen (globoside, Gb4)

P antigen receptors are present on what 3 cell types? 

 

●      Erythroid precursors, megakaryocytes, endothelial cells

In a healthy individual, what is the expected temporal pattern/effect on RBC production by parvo infection     

 

●      Transient aplastic crisis

○      Precipitous drop in hemoglobin

○      4-8 day cessation of red cell production

○      Hemoglobin drops ~ 1g/dL in normal individuals

○      Immune response develops against virus

○      Anemia resolves in 10-19 days

●      Chronic infection with persistent anemia occurs in immunocompromised individuals

○      Primary infection, reinfection or reactivation

 

Parvovirus presentation in healthy individuals

 

●      Self limiting disease in healthy individuals

●      Subclinical erythroid aplasia followed by rash or arthralgias

 

Microscopic Parvovirus infection in the BM

 

●      Minimal erythroid maturation beyond proerythroblast stage unless immunosuppressed

●      IHC for CD71, E-Cadherin

●      Giant proerythroblasts or "lantern cells" are hallmark of infection

 

 

 

●      Bone Marrow

○      Giant proerythroblasts are hallmark of B19V infection

■      Also referred to as "lantern cells"

○      Nuclei have fine megaloblastoid chromatin

○      Nuclear viral inclusions

○      Dark blue, often vacuolated cytoplasm in earliest cells

○      Become larger in size, lose cytoplasmic basophilia, and develop pseudopodia over time

○      Broad-based or "dog ear" cytoplasmic projections

 


What patients are at increased risk of Transient aplastic crisis in PB19 infection?   

 

●      Patients with hemolytic disorders (membranopathy, enzymopathy, hemoglobinopathy)

○      Hereditary spherocytosis

○      Thalassemia, sickle cell disease

○      Red cell enzyme deficiencies

○      Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

●      Patients with concurrent erythroid "stress”

○      Hemorrhage, iron deficiency anemia

○      Malaria, hookworm or other infections

●      Renal or stem cell transplant patients

 

Fetal infection - Highest risk time? Complications?

 

●      Highest risk in 11th-20th week gestation

●      Nonimmune hydrops fetalis

●      Rare abortions, average ~ 9% among infected women

Treatment for Parvo

●      Immunocompetent patients with transient aplastic crisis

○      Red blood cell transfusions

○      Supportive therapy

●      Immunosuppressed patients with persistent infection

○      Temporary cessation of immunosuppression if feasible

○      Administer intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg)

●      Arthralgias and arthritis

○      Respond to nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs

●      Maternal B19V infection

○      Intrauterine blood transfusions

○      Treatment of hydrops fetalis, severe fetal anemia

 

Zika

 

●      It is spread by daytime-active Aedes mosquitoes, such as A. aegypti and A. albopictus

●      Its name comes from the Zika Forest of Uganda, where the virus was first isolated in 1947

 

Zika Virus Clinical manifestations

 

-        Flu-like illness

-        Fever

-        Conjunctivitis

-        Swelling of hand/feet joints

 

How do you diagnose Zika

 

-        PCR

 

What is the deferral for Zika virus

Bacteria

Pertussis

●      Pertussis, also known as whooping cough, is a highly contagious respiratory disease. It is caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis

Microscopic features of Pertussis in the blood

●      Leukocytosis with lymphocytosis during early respiratory symptoms

●      WBC count may be > 50 x 10⁹/L for infants

●      Mature-appearing lymphocytes (primarily helper T cells)

●      Condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm

●      Many cleaved or convoluted nuclei

Tuberculosis

Microscopic features of Tuberculosis in BM

●      Discrete granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes, ± Langhans giant cells, scattered lymphocytes, ± caseation, neutrophils if immunocompromised (granulomas may be absent if immunocompromised)

●      Erythroid hypoplasia ± patchy-type necrosis

●      Detection of acid-fast organisms with ZN stain

Epithelioid cells with cuffing of lymphocytes

Many acid fast bacilli with slender forms are noted in the acid fast stain confirmatory of tubercular etiology

 

 

Anaplasma and Ehrlichia

 

What kind of organism is Ehrlichia?

 

●      Ehrlichiosis is the general name used to describe diseases caused by the bacteria Ehrlichia chaffeensis, E. ewingii, or E. muris eauclairensis

 

What kind of organism is Anaplasma?

 

●      Anaplasma is a genus of bacteria of the alphaproteobacterial order Rickettsiales

●      Anaplasma species reside in host blood cells and lead to the disease anaplasmosis.

●      The disease most commonly occurs in areas where competent tick vectors are indigenous, including tropical and semitropical areas of the world for intraerythrocytic Anaplasma spp.

 

What is the arthropod vector for Anaplasma and Ehrlichia?

 

●      Ticks

●      Ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis are similar tick-borne illnesses that cause flu-like symptoms, including fever, muscle aches and headache. Signs and symptoms of ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis usually appear within 14 days after a tick bite.

 

Which different WCs are infected by Anaplasma and Ehrlichia respectively?

 

●      Ehrlichiosis - Monocytes

●      Anaplasmosis - Neutrophils

 Monocytes from immunocompromised hosts may contain multiple morulae (Wright's stained blood film, patient 9, original magnification × 300).

Severe Anaplasmosis With Multiorgan Involvement in a Rheumatoid Arthritis Patient | Cureus

Rickettsioses, Q-fever

·       (caused by Coxiella burnetii), salmonelloses, borreliosis and brucellosis can be accompanied by a considerable BM lymphocytosis and (fibrin ring-) granulomas

·      Doughnut granulomas are highly evocative of Coxiella infections; however, they are not specific to Coxiella infections and have been seen in CMV, Epstein-Barr virus, Brucella and Salmonella infections, leishmaniasis, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, and immune disorders.

Lipogranulomatous bone marrow reaction in a patient suffering from proven complicated subacute borreliosis with reactive large granular lymphocytosis in the peripheral blood (being the reason to perform biopsy). Inset: CD68 staining of a small lipogranuloma in the same patient.

 

Borrelia

 

●      Borrelia is a genus of bacteria of the spirochete phylum

●      It causes Lyme disease, also called Lyme borreliosis, a zoonotic, vector-borne disease transmitted primarily by ticks and by lice, depending on the species of bacteria

●      Direct tests include culture of Borrelia from skin, blood, or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and detection of genetic material by polymerase chain reaction in skin, blood, or synovial fluid

●      Serological and immunological tests too - eg ELISA

 

 

Brucellosis

·       Can cause marrow granulomas, hemophagocytosis, and a peripheral pancytopenia

Trephine biopsy specimen of bone with normocellular bone marrow and a solitary epithelioid granuloma (hematoxylin and eosin stain, original magnification, × 150).

 

Tropheryma whippelli Whipple’s disease

·       PAS-positive organisms are seen within marrow macrophages

·       Confirmation can be accomplished by PCR or EM

Whipple disease involving the bone marrow. Note diastase-resistant PAS+ (foamy) interstitial histiocytes. Inset: presence of analogous histiocytes in a retroperitoneal lymph node of the same patient.

 

Salmonella typhi

·       Associated with pancytopenia due to hemophagocytosis, granulomas, ring granulomas, or bone marrow necrosis

Malaria (and Babesia)

 

Morphology of Malarial Parasites in Peripheral Blood Smears

 

Plasmodium falciparum

Enlarged (1.25x) (bc they invade immature RBCs), round to oval, ± fimbriated (like hair)

No

No

Black, in gametocytes

Gold/brown

Q. Which malarial species have macrocytosis?

 

●      Ovale & Vivax

 

Q. Which malarial species have schuffner dots?

 

●      Ovale & Vivax

 

Q. Differences between Ovale and Vivax? And Malariae? And Falciparum

 

Ovale:

-        Enlarged Oval RBC with FIMBRIATED edges

-        6-12 (fewer) merozoites per schizont

-        Merozoites in Rosette configuration (Rosettes kinda look like an “O”!)

-        Coarse Schuffner dots

-        Infects retics

 

Vivax

-        Enlarged Oval RBC WITHOUT fimbriated edges

-        12-24 (more) merozoites per schizont (Very increased in Vivax)

-        Merozoites in RANDOM configuration

-        Fine Schuffner dots

-        Infects retics

 

Malariae

-        Round RBC no fimbria, not enlarged

-        6-12 (fewer) merozoites per schizont

-        Merozoites may be in rosette configuration

-        No Schuffner dots

-        Infects mature RBC

-        THICK bands!

-        THICK rings

 

Falciparum

-        Normal RBC size

-        No Schizont

-        No Schuffner dots

-        Fine rings

-        Multiple rings per

-        Accole forms

-        Banana Gametocytes*

 

 

 

Name 4 malaria species, mention identifying morphologic features for each one of them which helps with differentiation, give two non-morphologic tests for speciation

 

Part 1: morphologic features

 

●      Macrocytic

o       Vivax:  RBC are enlarged, all stages of life cycle present, sometimes multiple parasites per cell [P. VIVAX TROPHOZOITES HAVE MORE PROMINENT AMEBOID FEATURES]

o       Ovale: RBC are enlarged, RBC are fimbriated, all stages but less so than than vivax, low parasitemia [P. OVALE SCHUFFNER DOTS COARSER, MORE NUMBEROUS, AND APPEAR EARLIER IN RING STAGE]

●      Normocytic

o       Falciparum: RBC are normal size, often multiple ring forms, usually only ring forms are seen, rings are smaller and delicate with “double dots” like a pair of headphones, aplicae forms, high parasitemia, crescent shaped gametocyte (“banana” shape) [DOUBLE CHROMATIN DOT RINGS ARE COMMON, MAURER DOTS BECOME RECOGNIZABLE IN TROPHOZOITES]

o       Malariae: RBC are normal size, No RBC changes, lowest parasitemia, all stages present [PRESENCE OF BAND FORM TROPHOITES]

●      Detection and identification of malarial parasites is facilitated if blood films are stained with a Giemsa stain at pH 7.2 (normal Wright Giemsa or MGG blood films are stained at pH of 6.8). Leishman stain may also be used (VGH)

o       At this pH P. vivax and P. ovale have different tinctorial qualities from non-parasitized cells

 

Part 2: non morphological tests

 

●      Non-morphological tests include PCR and immunochromatography

●      PCR

o       Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays are the most sensitive and specific method to detect malaria parasites

o       PCR-based assay detect parasite DNA

●      Immunochromatography:

o       Antigen detected = histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP2) is specific for P. falciparum pfLDH

o       Parasite LDH detects pan-malaria infection

o       Plasmodium aldolase (PMA) or parasite lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH)

o       Summary:

▪        3 possible antigens

●      Histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP2)-> P.f

●      Plasmodium aldolase (PMA)

●      Parasite lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH)-> Pan

o       Rheumatoid arthritis patients → may show false positive

o       Note these kits are less sensitive for ovale and malariae species

o       Note the sensitivity is generally 100 parasites per ul compared to expert microscopy 5-10 parasite per ul

 

●      Source: Bain Blood Cells 2nd edition p. 153

●      Source: Dacie and Lewis p.109

 

Note: although microscopy remains the gold standard diagnostic test for malaria in clinical settings, polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based assays can have 100-fold greater sensitivity, especially in the setting of low parasitemia or subclinical infections

 

 

2 stains for thick film?

 

●      Giemsa

●      Leishman

 

Thick film pH?

 

●      7.2 for Malaria to see → Schuffner dots (can use Giemsa or Lieshman stain)

 

What is the benefit of the thick film?

 

●      Higher concentration of parasites = incr. sensitivity

 

4 benefits of using a film vs rapid detection kit?

 

●      Rapid test cannot speciate (thin can)

●      Rapid test cannot quantitate

●      Rapid test will remain prolonged after infection cleared

●      Can miss co-infections

 

What is the method for quantifying malaria?

 

●      Thin film examination

 

Q. PCR for malaria?

 

●      Very sensitive

●      PCR is not quantitative

 

 

What other parasite may mimic malaria on a blood film?

 

●      Babesia

 

 Note: Be able to differentiate Falciparum from Babesia (below - note maltese cross)

 

 

 

·        Babesia ring forms in blood

o   See in 1-20% of RBCs

§  Up to 85% of RBCs in splenectomized individuals

·        Peripheral blood smear

o   Normal to slightly increased WBC count

o   Possible hemolytic anemia

o   Thrombocytopenia

·        Bone marrow

o   Increased erythropoiesis and hemophagocytosis

Two ring forms of Babesia are seen in this erythrocyte (black solid arrow). Rings are oval, round, or pear-shaped, and each has a chromatin dot. Differentiation from Plasmodium falciparum rings is difficult when distinctive features of Babesia are not present.

In high parasitemia, extracellular Babesia merozoites (black solid arrow) are found singly or in syncytial groups. Ring forms of P. falciparum are not observed outside of cells, except adjacent to recently destroyed erythrocytes.

Up to 12 rings (or Babesia merozoites) may be seen per red cell (black curved arrow). The distinctive finding of a Maltese cross, in which 4 merozoites coalesce and form a cross, is rare in Babesia microti infections.

 

 

 

 

Filaria

The Filarioidea are a superfamily of highly specialised parasitic nematodes. Species within this superfamily are known as filarial worms or filariae (singular "filaria"). Infections with parasitic filarial worms cause disease conditions generically known as filariasis.

 

What are the sheathed filaria vs unsheathed?

 

  1. Sheathed:
    1. Wuchereria bancrofti
    2. Loa loa
    3. Brugia malayi
  2. Unsheathed
    1. Mansonella perstans
    2. Mansonella ozzardi

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Leishmania

 

Leishmania is a genus of trypanosomes that are responsible for the disease leishmaniasis.

 

How is Leishmaniasis transmitted

 

-        Sand fly

 

What are the clinical features of Leishmaniasis

 

-        The disease can present in three main ways:

-        Cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral.

-        The cutaneous form presents with skin ulcers

-        The mucocutaneous form presents with ulcers of the skin, mouth, and nose.

-        The visceral form starts with skin ulcers and later presents with fever, low count of red blood cells, and enlarged spleen and liver.

-        Potential cause of massive splenomegaly (Kala-Azar)

 

Blood film findings in leishmaniasis?

 

●      Leishmaniasis is diagnosed in the hematology laboratory by direct visualization of the amastigotes (Leishman–Donovan bodies = specific round forms 2 to 4 mm in diameter - see image below).

 

 

●      Buffy-coat preparations of peripheral blood or aspirates from marrow, spleen, lymph nodes, or skin lesions should be spread on a slide to make a thin smear and stained with Leishman stain or Giemsa stain (pH 7.2) for 20 minutes.

●      Amastigotes are seen within blood and spleen monocytes or, less commonly, in circulating neutrophils and in aspirated tissue macrophages.

●      They are small, round bodies 2–4 μm in diameter with indistinct cytoplasm, a nucleus, and a small, rod-shaped kinetoplast. Occasionally, amastigotes may be seen lying free between cells

 

 

 

 

 

 

Trypanosoma

 

-        Trypanosoma is a genus of kinetoplastids (class Trypanosomatidae), a group of unicellular parasitic flagellate protozoa

-        Corkscrew-like motion

-        The majority of species are transmitted by blood-feeding invertebrates,

-        Tse Tse fly = vector of African trypanosomiasis

-        Know how to distinguish these morphologically

-        Know a bit about Chagas disease

 

 

 

 



 

 

 

 

 [QZ1]Chédiak–Higashi syndrome (CHS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that arises from a mutation of a lysosomal trafficking regulator protein, which leads to a decrease in phagocytosis. The decrease in phagocytosis results in recurrent pyogenic infections, albinism, and peripheral neuropathy.

 [QZ2]Griscelli syndrome (GS) is a rare autosomal recessive multisystem disorder of pigmentary dilution of skin, silver gray hair, variable immunodeficiency, neurological impairment, and abnormal accumulation of melanosomes in melanocytes.

 [QZ3]Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by oculocutaneous albinism, a bleeding diathesis, and other organ involvement specific to certain types [1-3]. Eleven types of HPS associated with mutations in 11 different genes have been recognized

 [QZ4]Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of rare disorders caused by mutations in different genes involved in the development and function of infection-fighting immune cells. Infants with SCID appear healthy at birth but are highly susceptible to severe infections.

 [QZ5]X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (XLP) is a disorder of the immune system and blood-forming cells that is found almost exclusively in males. More than half of individuals with this disorder experience an exaggerated immune response to the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

 [QZ6]Non-LCH, associated with juvenile chronic myelogenous leukemia (JMML), presents as a solitary red-brown, yellowish papule or nodule, most often on the head and neck area
